finding: Incomplete check: the shared web-search limit was reached before any parts prices could be loaded, so every parts figure is null and no full totals can be built. The live range of $180-$675 cannot be confirmed or corrected from our own numbers yet. What can be said: labor alone, at the stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks), comes to about $48-$400 for the economy example (2013 Civic, 0.4-2.5 hr) and the midsize example (2020 Outback, 0.4-2.5 hr), about $144-$400 for the truck/SUV example (2022 Durango, 1.2-2.5 hr) and about $120-$400 for the luxury example (1.0-2.5 hr); parts must be added to each. Against the benchmarks the live range looks about right: RepairPal's national average ($421-$566) sits inside it, Jerry's regulator-only figure ($138-$204) is below the live low, and J.D. Power's motor-only figure is $200-$300. Nothing found suggests the live range is badly off, but that is a comparison, not our own build. How solid the labor times are: the low ends for the economy, midsize and truck/SUV classes are manufacturer warranty times printed in dealer bulletins for the example vehicles themselves (Honda 0.4-0.5 hr for one front regulator and motor on the 2012-2013 Civic; Subaru 0.4 hr for one motor and regulator assembly on the 2020 Outback; FCA 1.2 hr to inspect, reseat and replace one regulator on the 2022-2023 Durango). Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill. The truck/SUV example is a three-row SUV because no full-size pickup bulletin with a printed regulator time was found (the GM and Ram bulletins loaded either refer to GM's published time or cover other parts). The luxury class has no manufacturer-stated time at all: its hours are general guide figures, not vehicle-specific. All high ends rest on one general repair guide's statement of 1.5-2.5 hours at a shop or dealer, supported by Jerry's 1-2 hours and J.D. Power's 2.1-hour average for a motor; J.D. Power also says some vehicles reach four to five hours. The Honda and Subaru times are for regulator and motor together, matching the unit; the FCA bulletins do not say whether the motor is included. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee (a dead window can also be a switch, fuse, wiring in the door jamb or a door module), door panel clips and a vapor barrier or sealant, window re-initialization or module programming on one-touch windows, shop supplies and sales tax. If the glass has dropped or come out of its channel, glass, run channel or clips may be added. Some vehicles sell the regulator and motor separately and a shop may replace only the failed one; the other side is quoted separately.
